tasks.title: tables t03: all per-seed tables
tasks.coverage_note:
I found no discrepancy in the four per-seed tables. I parsed all 80 rows (20 seeds x 2 q x T=3 and T=2) and recomputed every displayed cell from results/t3_r1/eval/per_run.csv. That is 600 cells: 280 in the two T=3 tables and 320 in the two T=2 tables. The 600 comprise Gmax_full_over_dw and EXP_root_over_dw at 5 decimals for bw, jt, jt_es, v20 and jt2, plus the bw and v20 run-gate verdicts and the jt2 G-A, G-F and G-S marks. All 600 string-match my own formatting of the CSV values. I recomputed the gates from the 02_preregistration.md section 6 thresholds, which are identical to prereg_criteria.json.
- G-A: eta_T_over_dw <= 0.005, rmse_pos_T_over_eT0 <= 0.05, tail_mean_T_over_eT0 <= 0.02.
- G-F: Gmax_full_over_dw <= 0.01.
- G-N: |dev - final| <= 0.001 for both eta_T and Gmax_full.
- G-S: stage1_rel_err_abs <= 0.05, applied only at T=2.
Both the stored gate columns (gate_G_A, gate_G_F, gate_G_N, gate_G_S, gates_pass) and my recomputation agree with every table mark. The bw and v20 'run gates' cell is G-A and G-F and G-N for bw, with G-S added for v20. The jt2 G-A, G-F and G-S columns match too.

The table marks and the recomputed gates give these failures:
- bw q50 seeds 50504 (eta_T 0.00623) and 50517 (eta_T 0.00568) fail G-A on eta_T.
- bw q60 seeds 50514 (Gmax 0.05628) and 50517 (Gmax 0.01089) fail G-F.
- v20 q50 seed 30510 fails G-A (eta_T 0.00580).
- All other bw and v20 runs pass.

The closest value to any threshold is jt2 q60 seed 30510 at Gmax 0.009993 (table 0.00999, pass). No value equals a threshold, so inclusivity does not matter. No G-N difference is above 0.00075, so G-N passes everywhere. No displayed value sits within 0.0009 of a rounding boundary, so the 5-decimal digits are not sensitive to the rounding rule.

Other checks:
- All 200 per_run.csv rows have status done, exit code 0, valid and dev_valid true, and global_rng_ok true.
- There are no duplicate (wave, arm, q, seed) keys.
- Seeds are 50501-50520 for T=3 and 30501-30520 for T=2, as D1 requires.
- analysis/per_run_table.csv equals per_run.csv on both columns (max abs difference 0.0, 200 rows).
- The four blocks embedded in 04_t3_results.md (sections 3) and 05_t2_comparison.md (section 5) are line-for-line identical to the fragment files.
- The prose gate counts in 05_t2_comparison.md line 18 that follow from these tables are consistent with them: jt2 G-F 9/20 and 4/20, G-S 15/20 and 14/20, and v20 seed 30510 failing G-A at 0.00580.

Not checked: the headings of the rest of the reports, the statistics outside the t03 tables, and the figures. I did not rerun the evaluation, so I rely on per_run.csv as the primary file and did not re-derive its values from the npz or run files.

These are the bins, and they carry all 17 flags (7 at q50, 10 at q60). jt and jt2 contribute 0 cells. The 14.15 expectation (5240 x 0.0027) pools the stratum cells and the bin cells.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Say that the cells are bw strata (200, 0 flags) plus jt_es bins (5040, 17 flags: 7 at q50, 10 at q60), and that jt and jt2 have none. Report the expectation for the jt_es bins separately (5040 x 0.0027 = 13.6).

I reproduced the decomposition from the primary files. results/t3_r1/launch_checks.json holds a per-run z_cells and z_flags for each of the 160 runs, and tools/t3/t3_launch_checks.py shows how they are computed. Summed per arm they give bw 200 cells and 0 flags, jt_es 5040 cells and 17 flags, and jt and jt2 0 cells (their launch checks do no z test). The total is 5240 cells and 17 flags, as the report says.

The two kinds of cell are real. For bw, _check_bw tests the run's totals of n_start_tail, n_start_near and n_start_mid per stage (stages 3 and 2) against the bin-balanced strata shares. Cells with p equal to 0 or 1 are skipped, so a run has 5 cells, not 6: stage 2 has no tail stratum (04_t3_results.md:483 says so). These are strata, not bins. For jt_es, _check_joint tests every bin of stage{2,3}_direct_es.

I recomputed the jt_es z values directly from visitation.npz for the 40 jt_es runs. Bin counts are 40 and 80 at q50 and 44 and 88 at q60. That gives 2400 cells with 7 flags at q50 and 2640 cells with 10 flags at q60, so 5040 cells with 17 flags. All 17 flags are in jt_es and none is in bw.

- labels the 5240 cells as "z per stage and bin", which is wrong for the 200 bw cells (strata);
- never says which arms the cells belong to, or that jt and jt2 have none;
- uses a pooled expectation of 5240 x 0.0027 = 14.15.

The jt_es expectation alone is 5040 x 0.0027 = 13.61, and the bw expectation is 200 x 0.0027 = 0.54.

The pooled sum 14.15 is arithmetically correct. The PI prompt (line 621) asks only for the count of |z| > 3 next to 0.0027 per cell, and no wrong conclusion follows from the pooling (17 against 13.6 or 14.15, and 0 against 0.54 for bw). So this is a labelling and scope imprecision, not a wrong number. verdict.reasoning:
The overreach exists. 04_t3_results.md:49 gives "the machine was shared (load average 9.9 at the start; ...)" as the reason the launch took 34 minutes instead of the pre-registered 22. The 34 minutes are right, but the data do not support that explanation. I re-derived the following from the primary files.

1. Duration. The launch record `launch_t3_t2j_20261017_010337.json` and `launch_exit.txt` give a start of 01:03:37 and an end of 01:37:41, so 34 min 04 s.

2. Slowdown per arm. From the per-run `wall_sec` in the launch record, the mean wall times are:
   - bw: 575 (q50) and 586 (q60), against 390 and 402 in the smoke record, about 1.46-1.49x.
   - jt: 495 and 493, against 339 and 341, about 1.46x.
   - jt_es: 571 and 573, against 389 and 390, about 1.47x.
   - jt2: 307 (q50) and 256 (q60), against 206 and 208, 1.48x and 1.24x.
   Summed `wall_sec` over the 160 runs is 21.4 h. The smoke means (396, 340, 390 and 207 s) scaled to 40 runs per arm give about 14.8 h. So the slowdown is a uniform factor of roughly 1.5 over the smoke basis, and the launch really did run slower than the estimate.

3. Background load does not separate the two waves. `loadavg_at_start` is 9.86 / 9.46 / 9.65 for this launch and 12.31 / 11.85 / 11.08 for the smoke wave (`smoke/launch_20261016_224126.json`, also 03_checks.md:72). Other users' load at the start was therefore lower in the slow launch than in the fast smoke wave. The 22-minute estimate was built from the smoke wall times, so it already included the smoke wave's background load.

4. What differs between the waves. The smoke wave ran 8 workers and this launch ran 40 (`workers` in both records). The machine has 64 logical CPUs on 2 sockets x 16 cores x 2 threads, so 32 physical cores. 8 workers plus about 12 of other load fits within 32 physical cores. 40 workers plus other users' load does not. The launch's own concurrency therefore sits at least as well as other users' load, and nothing in the repo tests either.

5. CPU time rose with wall time. The 04 cost table gives CPU time of 493 s (jt q50), 566 s (jt_es) and 529 s (bw), against 336, 385 and 353 s in the smoke wave. Per-run CPU time rose by the same factor of about 1.5, and CPU is within 2 % of wall for jt and jt_es. If other users' processes had taken the workers' CPU slots, wall time would rise while CPU time stayed flat. A uniform per-instruction slowdown (shared hyperthread cores, cache or memory bandwidth) is what the data show, and the 40 workers can produce that on their own.

6. The pre-registration. 02_preregistration.md:135 says the estimate assumed "no contention beyond what the smoke wave saw". The launch used 5 times the smoke wave's concurrency, so that assumption did not hold, and the report does not say so.

confirmed.claim: "G" is the full-domain gain of a one-stage deviation, "Delta" the gain at the stage's own policy
confirmed.truth: The definitions are swapped. In utils/v2_metrics.py:11-14 and utils/dp_br_verifier.py (v_br, v_mean, delta), G_t(d) = V_t^BR(d) - V_t^mean(d). Here the deviator re-optimises at stage t and at every later stage, so G is the gain of a dynamic best response. Delta_t(d) is the one-step deviation gap: deviate at stage t only, then continue with the policy's mean continuation. The prompt D6 items 1-2 say the same (G = gain of a dynamic best response; Delta_t = largest one-step deviation gain). At the terminal stage the two coincide, which is why G_max,3 = eta_3 in the section 4 table.
confirmed.suggested_fix: "G" is the gain of a dynamic best response (the deviator re-optimises at the stage and at every later stage); "Delta" is the one-step deviation gain (deviate at the stage only, then follow the policy).

verdict.reasoning:
I reproduced the problem from the code, the prompt and the per-run CSV. Line 3 of 04_t3_results.md says '"G" is the full-domain gain of a one-stage deviation, "Delta" the gain at the stage's own policy'. That definition of G is wrong.

1. Code. In utils/dp_br_verifier.py (lines ~381-418), v_br is built with the continuation W_br from v_br_next. The deviator re-optimises at stage t and at every later stage, so this is a dynamic best response. v_mean is the value of the policy's own mean chain. delta is vdev - v_mean, where vdev uses the continuation W_mean: deviate at stage t only, then follow the policy's mean continuation. That is the one-step (one-stage) deviation gap. utils/v2_metrics.py line 436 sets G = s.v_br - s.v_mean. Its docstring (lines 9-14) says v_br is "the deviator re-optimizes at t and at every later stage", delta is the "one-step gap Delta_t(d)", and G_t is "the full dynamic deviation gain".

2. Prompt. D6 item 1 in 25_t3_r1_prompt.md reads "G_t(d) = V_t^BR(d) - V_t^mean(d), the gain of a dynamic best response". D6 item 2 reads "Delta_max_t{t}_over_dw (η_t), the largest one-step deviation gain at stage t".

3. Data. In results/t3_r1/eval/per_run.csv, across all 120 rows (arms bw, jt, jt_es), G_max_t3_over_dw equals Delta_max_t3_over_dw exactly (max difference 0.0). At stages 1 and 2, G_max exceeds Delta_max in all 120 rows (max gaps 0.0169 and 0.0530), and Delta never exceeds G. A "one-stage deviation" gain cannot be larger than the dynamic-best-response gain, so this is what G = dynamic BR and Delta = one-step deviation predicts. It also explains why G_max,3 = eta_3 at the terminal stage.

4. Report wording. The phrase "full-domain gain of a one-stage deviation" is the definition of Delta, not of G. The phrase "Delta the gain at the stage's own policy" does not say it is the one-step deviation gain, so the roles are effectively swapped. The report's own later wording ("eta_3/dW (maximum stage-3 deviation gain)") is not affected. The line 3 sentence still points readers to the wrong definition of G and drops the dynamic (all later stages) feature on which the 'full-domain / Gmax_full' findings and the P2 argument rest. This is a wrong definition, not a rounding.

The checker's wording 'swapped' is slightly strong. G is clearly mis-described. Delta is described vaguely rather than with G's definition. The suggested fix is correct.

confirmed.claim: The launch took 34 minutes (01:03:37 to 01:37:41 UTC), against the pre-registered estimate of 22 minutes: the machine was shared (load average 9.9 at the start; ...)
confirmed.truth: The times are right (01:03:37 to 01:37:41 = 34 min 4 s; the estimate was 22 min). The cause is not tested. Per-run wall times were about 40-48 % above the 8-worker smoke wave (median 494 s for jt against 336-338 s, 583 s for bw against 387-399 s, 284 s for jt2 against 202-204 s). Process CPU time equals wall time in the launch (jt seed 50501: wall 499.0 s, CPU 498.4 s), so the runs were not waiting for a CPU. A load of 9.9 at the start shows other processes. The end-of-launch loads (38.0 and 41.3) are about what the launch's own 40 workers produce. The slowdown is equally consistent with 40-way self-contention (shared cores, memory bandwidth) against the smoke's 8 workers, so "the machine was shared" is a hypothesis, not an established cause.
confirmed.suggested_fix: State the numbers and drop the causal clause, or write "possibly because the machine was shared (load 9.9 at the start) or because 40 workers run slower per run than the 8 of the smoke wave; not separated".

verdict.reasoning:
I reproduced the problem from the primary files. The report's times and loads are right, but the colon in 04_t3_results.md:49 presents "the machine was shared" as the reason for the excess over the estimate, and the data do not test that.

1. The times check out. The launch started 01:03:37 (launch_t3_t2j_20261017_010337.json) and ended 01:37:41 (launch_exit.txt), which is 34 min 4 s. The estimate of about 22 minutes is in 03_checks.md:91 and 02_preregistration.md:135. The launch record gives load at start 9.86 / 9.46 / 9.65 and at end 18.8 / 38.0 / 41.3, matching the report's table.

2. The slowdown is per run, not queueing. I recomputed wall times from the launcher's per-run records in launch_stdout.txt. Medians in the launch were jt 494 s, jt_es 572 s, bw 583 s and jt2 284 s. Medians in the 8-worker smoke wave (smoke_cost.csv) were jt 336-338 s, jt_es 386-387 s, bw 387-399 s and jt2 202-204 s. That is about 40-48 % longer per run.

3. The runs were not waiting for a CPU. In every joint_run_summary.json, process CPU time equals wall time. For jt seed 50501, q50, wall was 499.0 s and CPU 498.4 s. The median CPU/wall ratio is 0.994-0.997 for jt, jt_es and jt2, and the minimum is 0.984. The smoke wave also had CPU equal to wall (jt: 335.7 s CPU against 336.3 s wall). So the same computation took about 48 % more CPU seconds. Scheduler waiting does not explain that. A per-core slowdown does, and that fits both hypotheses.

4. The smoke wave was also shared, so sharing alone does not explain the difference. Its load was 12.3 / 11.9 / 11.1 at the start and 15.7 / 16.1 / 13.6 at the end (03_checks.md:72). The launch started at a lower 9.9. The pre-registration says the estimate assumes "no contention beyond what the smoke wave saw" (02_preregistration.md:135).

5. The one clear difference between smoke and launch is the worker count, 8 against 40. /proc/cpuinfo shows Xeon Gold 6242 with 16 cores per socket and 32 siblings, so nproc = 64 is 32 physical cores with hyper-threading. Forty single-threaded workers plus other users' roughly 10 load share physical cores and memory bandwidth, which would slow each run with no help from other users.

6. The end-of-launch loads cannot separate the hypotheses. Inverting the 15-minute average (41.3 after 34 min, starting from 9.6) gives an effective mean load of about 45, which is roughly the launch's own 40 workers plus a modest remainder. The report's own parenthetical concedes that 38.0 and 41.3 "include this launch's 40 workers". (1) The number is correct. I recomputed the paired differences from results/t3_r1/eval/per_run.csv (Gmax_full_over_dw, bw minus jt_es, q=60). I used the pre-registered bootstrap: default_rng(20261016).integers(0,20,size=(10000,20)) with np.percentile at 0.625 and 99.375. The 98.75 % upper end is -3.38e-05, which matches criterion.csv and rounds to -0.00003. The report's "-0.00003" is right.

(2) "The smallest ... of the differences" depends on which differences are meant.
- 06_decision_inputs.md:44 sits in a four-row table. The sentence introducing it says "All four are statements about the mean paired difference", and it drops the qualifier "three" from 04_t3_results.md:213 ("the smallest of the three differences").
- My recomputation of the mean differences gives: H1 -0.18054 (q=50) and -0.10019 (q=60); H2 -0.01115 and -0.00896; H3 -0.16939 and -0.09122; H1-T2 -0.00923 and -0.01248.

- At q=60, H2 is the smallest of all four. Averaged over the two q, H2 (0.01006) is also below H1-T2 (0.01085).
- So "smallest" holds for the three T=3 hypotheses, at q=60, and on the q-average. It does not hold at q=50 against H1-T2, and the sentence does not say which reading it means.

(3) "Least tight" is ambiguous. The width and distance numbers below come from the pre-registered bootstrap.
- By 95 % interval width, H2 is the tightest of the T=3 trio, not the loosest. Its widths are 0.0037 (q=50) and 0.0106 (q=60). H1's are 0.098 and 0.049, and H3's are 0.098 and 0.045.

- The parenthetical "98.75 % interval at q = 60 reaches -0.00003" shows that distance from zero is meant, but only at q=60. A reader who takes "tight" as interval width would find the sentence contradicted by the data.

The suggested fix is reasonable. Severity is low: no number is wrong, and the imprecision is in the scope and meaning of two comparative words.
